steps.text: In an experiment you measure a value \(y\) at four times \(t\):
steps.explanation:
The values rise roughly evenly. You suspect a linear relationship
\(y = c_0 + c_1 t\)
and want to determine the two parameters \(c_0\) (intercept) and \(c_1\) (slope).

The problem: in general no line passes through four points. Measurements always scatter a little. So we are looking for the line that fits “best”.
steps.insight: Least squares fitting: a model with few parameters should fit many (inexact) measurements as well as possible.

steps.text: Let's write the requirement “the line passes through all points” as a linear system for \(c_0, c_1\):
steps.explanation:
Four equations, two unknowns: the system is overdetermined. The matrix \(A\) is \(4 \times 2\) – more rows than columns.

The first column of \(A\) consists of ones (it belongs to \(c_0\)), the second contains the times \(t_i\) (it belongs to \(c_1\)).

The first two equations give \(c_0 = 1\), \(c_1 = 1\). But then the third equation says \(1 + 2 = 3 \neq 2\). There is no exact solution.
steps.insight: Overdetermined system \(Ax \approx b\): more equations than unknowns, usually no exact solution.

steps.text: If there is no exact solution, we look for the one with the smallest deviations. Each measurement has a residual: the difference between measured value and model.
steps.formula: r_i = y_i - (c_0 + c_1 t_i), \qquad \text{goal: } \; \sum_i r_i^2 = \|r\|_2^2 \; \text{ minimal}
steps.explanation:
The animation shows the residuals as vertical bars between point and line. We minimise the sum of their squares. That is why the method is called least squares. It was invented by Carl Friedrich Gauss, who used it in 1801 to predict the orbit of the dwarf planet Ceres.

Why squares?
• Positive and negative deviations do not cancel each other.
• Large deviations are penalised more than small ones.
• The sum is differentiable – and its minimum leads, as we will see shortly, to a linear system.
steps.insight: Method of least squares: choose the parameters so that the sum of squared residuals is minimal.

steps.text: In general, the linear least squares problem reads:
steps.explanation:
In our example \(x = (c_0, c_1)\), \(b = (1, 2, 2, 4)\), \(m = 4\) measurements, \(n = 2\) parameters.

In this lesson you will learn two ways to solve it:
1. The normal equations: fast and simple, but numerically delicate.
2. The QR decomposition: somewhat more work, but stable – the standard in practice.

In between we will see exactly why way 1 can fail. At the end come Householder reflections, which computers use to compute the QR decomposition.
steps.insight: Linear least squares problem: \(\min \|Ax - b\|_2\) with more rows than columns.

steps.text: We are looking for the minimum of the function
steps.explanation:
This is a function of two variables. At the minimum both partial derivatives must be zero (as for extrema in calculus).

Differentiating with the chain rule:
• \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial c_0} = \sum_i 2\,(c_0 + c_1 t_i - y_i) \cdot 1 = 0\)
• \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial c_1} = \sum_i 2\,(c_0 + c_1 t_i - y_i) \cdot t_i = 0\)

The factors \(2\) can be dropped.
steps.insight: At the minimum all partial derivatives of the sum of squares vanish.

steps.text: Sorting the two conditions by \(c_0\) and \(c_1\) gives an ordinary \(2 \times 2\) linear system:
steps.explanation:
The first equation comes from \(\sum (c_0 + c_1 t_i - y_i) = 0\): the sum \(\sum c_0\) over \(m\) points is \(m \cdot c_0\).

The second comes from \(\sum t_i (c_0 + c_1 t_i - y_i) = 0\).

So only four sums from the data are needed: \(\sum t_i\), \(\sum t_i^2\), \(\sum y_i\), \(\sum t_i y_i\).
steps.insight: For the regression line you only need the sums \(\sum t_i\), \(\sum t_i^2\), \(\sum y_i\) and \(\sum t_i y_i\).

steps.text: Let's compute the sums for our measurements:
steps.explanation:
With \(m = 4\) the linear system is:
\(4\,c_0 + 6\,c_1 = 9\)
\(6\,c_0 + 14\,c_1 = 18\)

Exam tip: such a table is the clearest way to compute the sums without mistakes.
steps.insight: First set up a table with \(t_i\), \(y_i\), \(t_i^2\), \(t_i y_i\), then add up.

steps.text: Now we solve the \(2 \times 2\) system:
steps.explanation:
The regression line is \(y = 0.9 + 0.9\,t\).

Residuals (measured value minus line):
• \(t = 0\): \(1 - 0.9 = 0.1\)
• \(t = 1\): \(2 - 1.8 = 0.2\)
• \(t = 2\): \(2 - 2.7 = -0.7\)
• \(t = 3\): \(4 - 3.6 = 0.4\)

Sum of squares: \(0.01 + 0.04 + 0.49 + 0.16 = 0.70\).

For comparison, the line \(y = 1 + t\) through the first two points: residuals \(0, 0, -1, 0\), sum of squares \(1\). Our regression line is better, although it hits no point exactly.
steps.insight: The regression line does not have to hit any measurement exactly – it minimises the total error.

steps.text: The same system can be written compactly with the matrix \(A\). Check it:
steps.explanation:
These are exactly the sums from before: the top left entry is “ones times ones” \(= m\), top right “ones times \(t\)” \(= \sum t_i\), bottom right “\(t\) times \(t\)” \(= \sum t_i^2\).

So in general the system reads:
\(A^{T}A\,x = A^{T}b\)

These are the normal equations. They hold for every linear least squares problem, not just for lines.
steps.insight: Normal equations: \(A^{T}A\,x = A^{T}b\). The overdetermined \(m \times n\) system becomes a square \(n \times n\) system.

steps.text: Why “normal” equations? The word means “perpendicular” here. The equations say: the residual is perpendicular to all columns of \(A\).
steps.explanation:
Geometrically: all possible vectors \(Ax\) form a plane (the column space of \(A\)). The vector \(b\) does not lie in this plane. The point of the plane closest to \(b\) is the orthogonal projection – like dropping a perpendicular from a point onto a plane. The animation shows the projection of a vector onto a line; the principle is the same.

Check in the example with \(r = (0.1, 0.2, -0.7, 0.4)\):
• Column 1 (ones): \(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.7 + 0.4 = 0\) ✓
• Column 2 (\(t\)): \(0 + 0.2 - 1.4 + 1.2 = 0\) ✓
steps.insight: The solution of the least squares problem is the orthogonal projection: the residual is perpendicular to the column space of \(A\).

steps.text: When is the solution unique? When the columns of \(A\) are linearly independent (full column rank). Then:
steps.explanation:
• \(A^{T}A\) is invertible, the normal equations have exactly one solution.
• \(A^{T}A\) is even symmetric positive definite, because \(x^{T}A^{T}Ax = \|Ax\|_2^2 > 0\) for \(x \neq 0\).
• So the normal equations can be solved with the Cholesky decomposition (see “Gaussian Elimination & LU Decomposition”).

When are the columns dependent? For example, if all measurements were taken at the same time: then the \(t\) column is a multiple of the column of ones and no slope can be determined.
steps.insight: Full column rank ⇒ \(A^{T}A\) is spd ⇒ unique solution, computable with Cholesky.

steps.text: Quick check: you want to approximate the measurements \(y_1, \ldots, y_m\) by a constant \(y = c\). What do the normal equations give?
steps.explanation:
The model has only one parameter, \(A\) is a column of ones.
• \(A^{T}A = 1 + 1 + \ldots + 1 = m\)
• \(A^{T}b = y_1 + \ldots + y_m\)
• So \(c = \frac{y_1 + \ldots + y_m}{m}\) – the mean!

The mean is thus the “least squares constant”: it minimises the sum of squared deviations. For our data: \(c = \frac{9}{4} = 2.25\).
steps.insight: The mean is the solution of the simplest least squares problem.

steps.text: The method works for every model that is linear in its parameters. Example: a least squares parabola \(y = c_0 + c_1 t + c_2 t^2\) through the points \((-1, 3), (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 4)\).
steps.explanation:
The columns of \(A\) are \(1\), \(t_i\) and \(t_i^2\). That \(t^2\) is quadratic in \(t\) does not matter – what matters is that the parameters \(c_0, c_1, c_2\) appear only linearly.

Solution of the normal equations (e.g. with Gauss):
\(c_0 = 0.85\), \(c_1 = -0.95\), \(c_2 = 1.25\)

Residuals: \(-0.05,\ 0.15,\ -0.15,\ 0.05\). Check: their sum is \(0\) ✓ (perpendicular to the column of ones).
steps.insight: “Linear” means: linear in the unknown parameters. The functions of \(t\) can be arbitrary.

steps.text: Some nonlinear models can be made linear by rewriting. Example growth: \(y = a\,e^{bt}\). Taking logarithms gives:
steps.explanation:
This is a line in the parameters \(\ln a\) and \(b\)!

Measurements: \((0;\ 2.0)\), \((1;\ 5.5)\), \((2;\ 14.7)\).
1. Take logarithms: \(\ln y \approx 0.693,\ 1.705,\ 2.688\)
2. Regression line through \((t_i, \ln y_i)\): \(\ln a \approx 0.698\), \(b \approx 0.997\)
3. Transform back: \(a = e^{0.698} \approx 2.01\)

Model: \(y \approx 2.01\, e^{0.997\, t}\).

Small catch: this minimises the errors of \(\ln y\), not of \(y\). For accurate results nonlinear methods are used (Gauss–Newton, see “Newton's Method for Systems”).
steps.insight: Exponential models become lines by taking logarithms.

steps.text:
Quick check: which models can be fitted with linear least squares directly (or after a simple transformation)?
• \(y = a + b \sin t\)
• \(y = a\,t^{b}\)
• \(y = \frac{a}{1 + b\,t}\)
steps.explanation:
• \(y = a + b \sin t\): directly linear in \(a\) and \(b\). Columns: \(1\) and \(\sin t_i\).
• \(y = a\,t^{b}\): after taking logarithms \(\ln y = \ln a + b \ln t\) – a line in \(\ln t\).
• \(y = \frac{a}{1 + b t}\): not linear in the parameters. A nonlinear method is needed here. (One could look at \(\frac{1}{y}\), but that distorts the errors even more.)
steps.insight: First check whether the model is linear in the parameters or can be transformed to be.

steps.text: The normal equations are elegant and cheap. Still, professional software rarely uses them. The reason is conditioning:
steps.explanation:
Why? The singular values of \(A\) (semi-axes of the image ellipse) are squared in \(A^{T}A\): \(\sigma_{\max}^2\) and \(\sigma_{\min}^2\). So the ratio is squared.

The consequence, by the rule of thumb from “Norms & Matrix Condition”:
• \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = 10^{3}\): via \(A^{T}A\) you lose 6 instead of 3 digits – usually still fine.
• \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = 10^{6}\): you lose 12 instead of 6 digits – only 4 remain.
• \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = 10^{8}\): \(A^{T}A\) has condition number \(10^{16}\) – no result can be trusted.

In polynomial least squares with high degree, condition numbers of \(10^{6}\) and more are completely normal.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The problem with the normal equations
steps.insight: The normal equations square the condition number – and thereby double the loss of significant digits.

steps.text: A dramatic example. With \(\delta = 10^{-8}\) consider
steps.explanation:
The columns of \(A\) are clearly linearly independent – \(A\) has full rank, \(\operatorname{cond}_2(A) \approx 1.4 \cdot 10^{8}\). That is large, but still solvable in double (about 8 digits remain).

But: \(\delta^2 = 10^{-16}\) is smaller than the unit roundoff. On a computer, therefore, \(1 + \delta^2 = 1\), and we get
\(\operatorname{fl}(A^{T}A) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\)

This matrix is singular! The normal equations cannot be solved, although the least squares problem has a unique solution. The information was in \(\delta\) – and was swallowed when forming \(A^{T}A\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The problem with the normal equations
steps.insight: Even forming \(A^{T}A\) can destroy information. Better: work with \(A\) directly.

steps.text: How can the least squares problem be solved without forming \(A^{T}A\)? The idea: transform \(A\) in a way that preserves the 2-norm of the residual but brings the system into triangular form.
steps.explanation:
In Gauss we subtracted rows. But that changes lengths – and \(\|Ax - b\|_2\) is a length.

We need transformations that do not change lengths: rotations and reflections. In matrix language: orthogonal matrices.

Plan: \(A = QR\) with orthogonal \(Q\) and upper triangular \(R\). Then the least squares problem becomes a triangular system.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The problem with the normal equations
steps.insight: Idea of the QR method: bring the system into triangular form using length-preserving transformations (rotations, reflections).

steps.text: A square matrix \(Q\) is called orthogonal if its columns are pairwise perpendicular and have length \(1\). In short:
steps.explanation:
The inverse is simply the transpose – that is what makes orthogonal matrices so pleasant.

Examples:
• Rotation by the angle \(\varphi\): \(\begin{pmatrix} \cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi \end{pmatrix}\)
• Reflection in the \(x_1\) axis: \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\)

Check for the rotation with \(\varphi = 90°\): \(Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), \(Q^{T}Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = I\) ✓
steps.insight: Orthogonal matrix: \(Q^{T}Q = I\). Examples are rotations and reflections.

steps.text: The decisive property: orthogonal matrices do not change lengths.
steps.explanation:
A rotation or reflection moves a vector, but it keeps its length.

Consequences:
• \(\|Q\|_2 = 1\) and \(\|Q^{-1}\|_2 = \|Q^{T}\|_2 = 1\), so \(\operatorname{cond}_2(Q) = 1\) – the best possible conditioning.
• Rounding errors are not magnified by \(Q\).
• For the least squares problem: \(\|Ax - b\|_2 = \|Q^{T}(Ax - b)\|_2\). You may multiply by \(Q^{T}\) without changing the minimum.
steps.insight: Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and have condition number 1 – ideal for stable algorithms.

steps.text: The QR decomposition writes an \(m \times n\) matrix \(A\) (with \(m \ge n\)) as
steps.explanation:
• \(Q\) is an orthogonal \(m \times m\) matrix.
• \(R\) is \(m \times n\) and has a square upper triangular matrix \(\hat{R}\) (\(n \times n\)) on top and only zeros below.

Often the reduced form \(A = \hat{Q}\hat{R}\) is enough, in which \(\hat{Q}\) contains only the first \(n\) columns of \(Q\) (\(m \times n\), orthonormal columns).

For our line example \(A\) is a \(4 \times 2\) matrix, so \(\hat{Q}\) is a \(4 \times 2\) matrix and \(\hat{R}\) a \(2 \times 2\) triangular matrix.
steps.insight: QR decomposition: \(A = QR\), \(Q\) orthogonal, \(R\) upper triangular (with zero rows at the bottom).

steps.text: This is how it solves the least squares problem:
steps.explanation:
Here \(Q^{T}b = \begin{pmatrix} c \\ d \end{pmatrix}\) with \(c\) (the first \(n\) entries) and \(d\) (the rest).

The second term \(\|d\|_2^2\) does not depend on \(x\) at all – nothing can be done about it. The first term can be made zero by solving the triangular system
\(\hat{R}x = c\)
by back substitution.

Bonus: the minimal sum of squares is exactly \(\|d\|_2^2\).
steps.insight: Solving with QR: compute \(c = \hat{Q}^{T}b\), then solve \(\hat{R}x = c\) backwards.

steps.text: Why is this better than the normal equations?
steps.explanation:
• \(A^{T}A\) is never formed. The information is not swallowed by squaring.
• The matrix \(\hat{R}\) has the same condition number as \(A\): \(\operatorname{cond}_2(\hat{R}) = \operatorname{cond}_2(A)\) – not the square.
• All transformations are orthogonal and do not magnify rounding errors.

The price: the QR decomposition costs about twice as much as setting up and solving the normal equations. For well-conditioned problems the normal equations are therefore fine – for ill-conditioned ones it has to be QR.
steps.insight: QR: \(\operatorname{cond}(\hat{R}) = \operatorname{cond}(A)\). Normal equations: \(\operatorname{cond}(A^{T}A) = \operatorname{cond}(A)^2\).

steps.text: How are \(Q\) and \(R\) computed? You know the most intuitive method from linear algebra: the Gram–Schmidt process. The columns of \(A\) are made orthonormal one after another.
steps.explanation:
In words:
1. Bring the first column to length \(1\).
2. From the second column subtract the part in direction \(q_1\) (the projection). What remains is perpendicular to \(q_1\). Then normalise.
3. With more columns: from each new column subtract the parts in the directions of all previous \(q_j\).

The subtracted coefficients and the lengths form the entries of \(\hat{R}\).
steps.insight: Gram–Schmidt: subtract the projections onto the previous directions, then normalise.

steps.text: Let's carry out Gram–Schmidt for our line example. The columns are \(a_1 = (1, 1, 1, 1)\) and \(a_2 = (0, 1, 2, 3)\).
steps.explanation:
Check that \(q_2\) is perpendicular to \(q_1\): \(-1.5 - 0.5 + 0.5 + 1.5 = 0\) ✓

The numbers for \(\hat{R}\):
• \(r_{11} = \|a_1\| = 2\)
• \(r_{12} = q_1^{T}a_2 = 3\)
• \(r_{22} = \|\tilde{q}_2\| = \sqrt{5}\)

So \(\hat{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5} \end{pmatrix}\). Read backwards: \(a_1 = 2q_1\) and \(a_2 = 3q_1 + \sqrt{5}\,q_2\) – exactly \(A = \hat{Q}\hat{R}\).
steps.insight: \(\hat{R}\) contains the projection coefficients on top and the lengths on the diagonal.

steps.text: Now we solve the least squares problem with this decomposition. First \(c = \hat{Q}^{T}b\) with \(b = (1, 2, 2, 4)\):
steps.explanation:
Then solve \(\hat{R}x = c\) backwards:
• \(\sqrt{5}\,x_2 = \frac{4.5}{\sqrt{5}} \Rightarrow x_2 = \frac{4.5}{5} = 0.9\)
• \(2\,x_1 + 3 \cdot 0.9 = 4.5 \Rightarrow x_1 = \frac{4.5 - 2.7}{2} = 0.9\)

Again \(c_0 = 0.9\), \(c_1 = 0.9\) – the same result as with the normal equations ✓. For this well-conditioned example both ways are equally good. The difference only shows for ill-conditioned problems.
steps.insight: QR and the normal equations give mathematically the same solution – numerically QR is more robust.

steps.text: A catch: the classical Gram–Schmidt process is itself numerically sensitive. If two columns are almost parallel, \(\tilde{q}_2 = a_2 - (\ldots)\,q_1\) is a difference of almost equal vectors – cancellation!
steps.explanation:
The computed \(q_j\) are then no longer really perpendicular to each other on the computer. This is called loss of orthogonality.

Remedies:
• Modified Gram–Schmidt: subtract the projections one after another from the already corrected vector instead of all from the original. Mathematically equal, numerically much better.
• Householder reflections (next chapter): they build \(Q\) from exactly orthogonal reflections and are the standard in practice.
steps.insight: Classical Gram–Schmidt loses orthogonality for almost parallel columns. In practice Householder is used.

steps.text: The Householder method works like Gauss: column by column, zeros are created below the diagonal. But instead of subtracting rows, reflections are used.
steps.explanation:
\(H\) reflects every vector in the plane (hyperplane) perpendicular to \(v\):
• A vector in direction \(v\) is reversed: \(Hv = -v\).
• A vector perpendicular to \(v\) stays unchanged.

\(H\) is symmetric and orthogonal: \(H^{T} = H\) and \(H^{2} = I\) (reflecting twice gives the original). That is why \(H\) is called a Householder reflection.
steps.insight: Householder matrix \(H = I - 2\frac{vv^{T}}{v^{T}v}\): reflection in the plane perpendicular to \(v\).

steps.text: Goal: a column \(a\) is to be reflected onto a multiple of the first unit vector \(e_1\) – then there are zeros below. Since reflections preserve lengths, the image must have length \(\|a\|\). The choice:
steps.explanation:
Example \(a = (3, 4)\): \(\|a\| = 5\), \(v = (3 + 5,\ 4) = (8, 4)\).

Check with \(Ha = a - \frac{2\,v^{T}a}{v^{T}v}\,v\):
• \(v^{T}a = 24 + 16 = 40\), \(v^{T}v = 64 + 16 = 80\)
• \(Ha = (3, 4) - \frac{2 \cdot 40}{80}(8, 4) = (3, 4) - (8, 4) = (-5, 0)\) ✓

The second component is \(0\), and the length \(5\) has been preserved. The animation shows this reflection.

Tip: you never have to write \(H\) out as a matrix. The formula \(Ha = a - \frac{2 v^{T}a}{v^{T}v} v\) is enough – that saves a lot of work.
steps.insight: Householder vector \(v = a + \operatorname{sign}(a_1)\|a\|e_1\). Then \(Ha\) is a multiple of \(e_1\).

steps.text: Why the sign \(\operatorname{sign}(a_1)\)? Mathematically \(v = a - \|a\|e_1\) would also work (reflection onto \(+\|a\|e_1\)).
steps.explanation:
But: if \(a\) is already almost a positive multiple of \(e_1\), say \(a = (1, 10^{-9})\), then \(\|a\| \approx 1\) and
\(a_1 - \|a\| \approx 1 - 1\) – cancellation!

With the sign of \(a_1\) we add instead: \(a_1 + \|a\| \approx 2\). No cancellation.

This is again the principle from “Floating-Point Numbers & Rounding Errors”: between two mathematically equivalent formulas, choose the one without a difference of nearly equal numbers.
steps.insight: The sign in \(v = a + \operatorname{sign}(a_1)\|a\|e_1\) prevents cancellation.

steps.text: An example in three dimensions: \(a = (2, 1, 2)\).
steps.explanation:
With a single reflection both entries below the first have become zero ✓

Gauss would have needed two row operations for that. The reflection handles the whole column at once – and preserves lengths.
steps.insight: One Householder reflection creates all the zeros below the diagonal element of a column in one step.

steps.text: The complete QR decomposition is built column by column, as with Gauss:
steps.formula: H_n \cdots H_2 H_1 A = R \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad A = \underbrace{H_1 H_2 \cdots H_n}_{=\,Q} R
steps.explanation:
1. \(H_1\) reflects the first column of \(A\) onto a multiple of \(e_1\).
2. \(H_2\) acts only on rows \(2\) to \(m\) and clears the second column below the diagonal. The first row and column stay unchanged.
3. And so on up to the last column.

Since each \(H_k\) is orthogonal (and \(H_k^{-1} = H_k\)), \(Q = H_1 H_2 \cdots H_n\) is orthogonal too.

Properties:
• Cost about \(2mn^2 - \frac{2}{3}n^3\) operations.
• Backward stable – without any pivoting.
• Standard in MATLAB, NumPy and LAPACK for least squares problems.
steps.insight: Householder QR: reflect column by column. Stable, no pivoting – the standard for least squares problems.

steps.text: An alternative to reflections are rotations, the Givens rotations. A Givens rotation makes exactly one entry zero.
steps.formula: \begin{pmatrix} c & s \\ -s & c \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} r \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, \quad c = \frac{a}{r}, \quad s = \frac{b}{r}
steps.explanation:
Example \((a, b) = (3, 4)\): \(r = 5\), \(c = 0.6\), \(s = 0.8\).
Check: \(0.6 \cdot 3 + 0.8 \cdot 4 = 1.8 + 3.2 = 5\) ✓ and \(-0.8 \cdot 3 + 0.6 \cdot 4 = -2.4 + 2.4 = 0\) ✓

So the vector is rotated so that it lands on the first axis.

When do you use Givens instead of Householder? When only a few entries have to be eliminated, for example for sparse matrices or when an already decomposed matrix is extended by one row. Givens rotations also reappear in the QR algorithm for eigenvalues.
steps.insight: Givens rotation: make a single entry zero by a rotation.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Formulate overdetermined systems \(Ax \approx b\) (more equations than unknowns) as the least squares problem \(\min \|Ax - b\|_2\).

2. Set up and solve the normal equations \(A^{T}Ax = A^{T}b\), for lines with the sums \(\sum t_i\), \(\sum t_i^2\), \(\sum y_i\), \(\sum t_i y_i\). Geometrically: the residual is perpendicular to the column space.

3. Fit models that are linear in the parameters (polynomials, \(a + b \sin t\)) and linearisable models (\(y = a e^{bt}\)).

4. Danger: \(\operatorname{cond}(A^{T}A) = \operatorname{cond}(A)^2\). Even forming \(A^{T}A\) can destroy information.

5. QR decomposition \(A = QR\): \(c = \hat{Q}^{T}b\), then \(\hat{R}x = c\). The condition number stays \(\operatorname{cond}(A)\).

6. Computing QR: Gram–Schmidt (intuitive but sensitive), Householder reflections \(v = a + \operatorname{sign}(a_1)\|a\|e_1\) (standard), Givens rotations (targeted single entries).
steps.insight: Key message: least squares problems are solved stably with Householder QR. Normal equations only for well-conditioned problems.

steps.text: What comes next? So far we have solved linear systems directly – with a fixed number of operations.
steps.explanation:
In the next lesson “Iterative Solvers for Linear Systems” we deal with huge sparse systems with millions of unknowns, where \(O(n^3)\) is no longer affordable. There one approaches the solution step by step – with Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel and the conjugate gradient method.

The ideas of this lesson come back later:
• Orthogonal transformations in the QR algorithm for eigenvalues (“Computing Eigenvalues”).
• Nonlinear least squares problems with the Gauss–Newton method (“Newton's Method for Systems”).
steps.insight: Orthogonal transformations are one of the most important tools of numerical linear algebra.
